chapter: Callers: Papa John Joseph to Congo Square
title: Joe Oliver's mute technique
summary: Wiggs explains Oliver's half-inserted mute and hand work compared with the plunger and wah-wah mute.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: You know, I want to ask you a question at this point. Whatever happened to the mute on the cornet and the trumpet? That's just passe, huh? But it sure sounded good. No, no.

It's still being used, but not, not as much as it, as it was before. Uh, you see, Joe Oliver used it in a way which was extremely effective, and none of our northern brethren know about that. The only thing the northern brethren know, uh, excuse me, people. Watch it now. We've got a lot of those Yankees in the city. Yeah, I know. I'm going to get it. Uh, well, they, they used a plunger, you know, which is oh so naughty and dirty. They put a mute in there, and then they put a plunger. Well, Joe Oliver didn't do that. Joe Oliver put a mute halfway in the horn, and he used his hand to, to manipulate, manipulate the, uh, uh, the, the wah-wows. And lo and behold, if some creature didn't invent a horrible wah-wah mute after that, you know, man, I'm going to get myself in more trouble. I think Patty Orman's dead now.
